Votre chien est atteint d’une tumeur orale maligne ?
L’équipe de Cancérologie de VetAgro Sup et le Centre d’Investigation Clinique Vétérinaire (CICV) mènent actuellement une étude en collaboration avec la société biopharmaceutique FINDIMMUNE, qui développe des thérapies anticancéreuses et immunitaires, afin de développer un nouveau médicament pour traiter les mélanomes et carcinomes épidermoïdes buccaux.
Détails de l'étude
L’étude consiste en l’administration intra-tumorale du médicament innovant. Cette recherche implique 10 visites sur le site de VetAgro Sup sur une durée de 6 mois. Une première visite de sélection est prévue au service de Cancérologie pour confirmer le diagnostic de votre chien. Le traitement prévoit 3 injections programmées à J1, J30 et J90, ainsi que des visites de suivi à J7, J15, J60, J120, J150 et J180.Votre chien aura accès gratuitement au traitement innovant et son suivi médical sera entièrement pris en charge.
A ce jour, il n’existe pas d’alternative médicamenteuse pour le traitement des tumeurs orales malignes. La participation de votre chien à cette étude ouvrira la voie à un nouveau traitement des mélanomes et carcinomes chez le chien. Cela améliorera considérablement la qualité de vie des chiens traités.Si vous souhaitez participer, n’hésitez pas à contacter le secrétariat des cliniques afin de prendre rendez-vous en Cancérologie au 0478872670 En cas de question sur cette étude, vous pouvez contacter le CICV : cicv@vetagro-sup.frNous vous remercions par avance de l’aide que vous pourrez nous apporter et de votre contribution.

There is an unmet need for effective treatments for canine B-cell lymphoma. The standard of care for dogs with B-cell lymphoma provides relatively short median overall survival times despite high remission rates. Side effects are common and may be dose-limiting.B-cell lymphoma occurs as a result of neoplastic transformation and clonal expansion of B-lymphocytes. Aberrant expression of multiple components of B-cell receptor (BCR) signaling has been demonstrated in canine B-cell lymphoma. Bruton’s tyrosine kinase (BTK) plays a crucial role in oncogenic signaling downstream of the BCR that is critical for the proliferation and survival of B-cells in many B-cell malignancies. The BTK inhibitor BI 705564 has the potential to achieve marked clinical responses in dogs with B-cell malignancies and addresses major unmet needs. These include the expected improvement of quality of life with minimal side effects, increased survival time, oral administration, and affordability. We are currently seeking patients for enrollment in funded oncology clinical trials. Study goals and suitability for each patient are discussed in detail with the clients prior to enrollment. Although clinical trial enrollment may not be the best option for all patients, in many cases, clinical trial participation provides the opportunity to receive novel, cutting-edge therapies free of charge or at a reduced cost and may facilitate treatment of pets where it would not otherwise be possible due to financial constraints or lack of other therapy options. Criteria for enrollment are outlined for each tumor type below. Please direct referrals or questions to the Oncology Clinical Trials Service at 573-882-7821.

Bruton’s Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitor (BI705564) for Canine B‑Cell Lymphoma
The University of Missouri Veterinary Health Center is enrolling dogs in a clinical trial evaluating an investigational oral Bruton’s Tyrosine Kinase (BTK) inhibitor—BI705564—for the treatment of newly diagnosed B‑cell lymphoma. This exploratory, multicenter field study aims to assess both efficacy and safety of BTK inhibition in canine patients.
Eligibility includes:
Dogs >1 year old and 10–50 kg in body weight
Naïve, untreated B‑cell lymphoma confirmed by cytology or histology with immunophenotyping (flow cytometry)
At least two peripheral lymph nodes ≥2 cm in longest diameter
WHO stage II, III, or IV B‑cell lymphoma
Adequate organ function on bloodwork and urinalysis
Performance score of 0–1 (normal to mildly decreased activity) and life expectancy ≥1 month
Owner consent
Key exclusions:
T‑cell lymphoma or involvement of skin, GI tract, or nervous system
Internal‑only disease (mediastinum, liver, spleen) without peripheral lymph node enlargement
Prior lymphoma treatment (chemotherapy, Tanovea, Laverdia, radiation) or long‑term corticosteroids (>2 weeks)
Hypercalcemia, MDR1 deficiency, pregnancy/lactation, or concurrent trial enrollment
Study overview:
Dogs will receive oral BI705564 once daily for 3 months (84 days) at 5 mg/kg, with possible dose escalation to 10 mg/kg in certain cases depending on early target occupancy results.
The study includes scheduled evaluations such as:
Physical examinations and lymph node measurements
Quality‑of‑life assessments
Bloodwork (CBC, chemistry, lymphoma testing)
Lymph node aspirates for target occupancy evaluation
Thoracic radiographs and abdominal ultrasound at screening
Follow‑up continues regularly throughout the 12‑week treatment period.
Potential benefits:
Access to a novel investigational BTK inhibitor designed to target B‑cell lymphoma
All study‑related diagnostics, monitoring, and investigational drug costs are covered
Opportunity to contribute to advancement of veterinary oncology and comparative cancer therapeutics
Potential risks:
Possible drug‑related side effects (as with any investigational therapy)
Risks associated with repeated lymph node aspirates, blood draws, and imaging procedures
Dogs may be withdrawn if adverse events occur or if continued participation is not in the animal’s best interest
Owner commitment:
Owners must agree to:
Bring their dog for all required study visits over 12 weeks
Administer oral medication daily as directed
Allow required diagnostic sampling (bloodwork, lymph node aspirates, imaging)
Participate in quality‑of‑life assessments
Dogs may be withdrawn at any time. If a dog passes away during the study, postmortem evaluation is requested to improve understanding of treatment effects.

COTC033: Repurposing Vaccine Immunity to Treat Cancers
The University of Missouri Veterinary Medical Center is enrolling patients into a clinical trial evaluating the safety and effectiveness of a new immunotherapy, the Vaccine Peptide Library (VPL), when given to dogs with cancer. Studies in dogs with cancer will complement current human trials designed to test new doses and effects of this agent.
Criteria:
Body weight between 15 and 60 kg
Tumor biopsy or cytology to confirm diagnosis
Solid tumor measuring 2 to 8 cm
No mast cell tumors, cutaneous hemangiosarcomas, thyroid carcinomas, or lymphomas
Must not have received ANY prior experimental therapy
No concurrent chemotherapy or radiation therapy – 2 week washout period required
No concurrent immunomodulatory therapy (including Apoquel or Cytopoint) – 6 week washout period required
No concurrent corticosteroids – 1 week washout period required
No hypercalcemia causing illness
No significant co-morbid illness, which includes, but is not limited to: pulmonary metastatic disease, renal or hepatic failure, history of congestive heart failure or clinical coagulopathy, autoimmune disorders, or uncontrolled endocrinopathies
Benefit:
Complete cost of all treatments and rechecks covered by study, include initial staging or adverse side effects.
This trial is being conducted concurrently with human trials.
Contribute to development of an important cancer therapy.
At the conclusion of the study, there will be a $1000 monetary gift provided towards additional treatment for your pet’s cancer.
To Participate:
Pet owners must be willing to transport their dog to and from the treatment center in Columbia, MO for every visit abiding by specific timelines.
A full screening will be performed prior to full study enrollment.
Participation will require a total of up to 13 weekly visits.
For more information on this study please contact: cvmclinicaltrials@missouri.edu with the subject pertaining to the trial of interest or fill out a short survey here.
Feline GI Lymphoma Radiation + Chemotherapy
The University of Missouri Veterinary Health Center is enrolling patients into a clinical trial evaluating the safety and efficacy of whole abdomen radiation therapy (WART) followed by a chemotherapy protocol (COP/Dox) in cats with spontaneous large cell GI lymphoma. This study will seek to better understand the effects of radiation therapy prior to receiving chemotherapy for this common feline cancer.
Criteria:
Feline patients with high grade lymphoma in the GI tract
Patients must have cytologically or histopathologically confirmed lymphoma
Patients must not have been previously treated with chemotherapy
Patients cannot be FeLV or FIV positive or have severe systemic disease that would place them at higher risk with general anesthesia.
Patients CANNOT have evidence of lymphoma outside of the abdomen.
Eligibility is at the discretion of the investigator.
Benefit:
The cost of the radiation portion of care (WART) will be covered by the study.
Your pet will contribute to development of an important cancer therapy.
Patient will receive $1,000 stipend for use at the VHC after completion of radiation therapy
To Participate:
Pet owners must be willing to transport their cat to and from the treatment center in Columbia, Missouri, for every visit abiding by specific timelines.
A full screening including a CBC (complete blood count), serum biochemistry panel, urinalysis, thoracic radiographs (x-rays), and abdominal ultrasound will be performed prior to full study enrollment.
Participation will require pets to come to our clinic weekly for a minimum of eight weeks and then every 3 weeks for 5 additional visits, with radiation administered the first week only.
For more information on this study please contact: cvmclinicaltrials@missouri.edu with the subject pertaining to the trial of interest.
Gilvetmab for the Treatment of Primary Pulmonary Carcinoma in Dogs
The University of Missouri Veterinary Medical Center is enrolling patients into a clinical trial evaluating the effectiveness of Gilvetmab, an anti-PD1 monoclonal antibody, as a treatment for canine pulmonary carcinoma. Similar treatments have been shown to improve survival in human lung cancer patients.
Criteria:
Dogs with gross disease and those with microscopic disease
No immune-mediated disease or other severe comorbidities
No concurrent use of steroids or other immunosuppressive drugs
Study Involvement:
Gilvetmab is given as a slow infusion every two weeks for up to 10 doses.
CBC, chemistry, and urinalysis are performed every 4 weeks.
Chest x-rays are performed every 8 weeks.
Benefit:
The study covers the cost of Gilvetmab treatment (ranges from $540 – $1350 per treatment, depending on patient size).
Owner is responsive for recheck exams, bloodwork, and x-rays.
To Participate:
Pet owners must be willing to transport their dog to and from the treatment center in Columbia, MO for every visit abiding by specific timelines.
A full screening will be performed prior to full study enrollment.
Participation will require a total of up to 10 biweekly visits.
For more information on this study please contact: cvmclinicaltrials@missouri.edu with the subject pertaining to the trial of interest or fill out a short survey here.
LEAH xCAR-T: Canine B-Cell Lymphoma
The University of Missouri Veterinary Medical Center is enrolling patients into a clinical trial evaluating the safety and efficacy of lymphodepleting chemotherapy and xenogenic CAR-T cell therapy in dogs with spontaneous CD20+ lymphoma. CAR-T cells are lymphocytes (immune cells) that have had a series of genes added to them that make them professional killers of any cell carrying the target molecule. This study will seek to better understand the effects of the CAR-T cells on the tumor as well as the dog’s immune system.
Criteria:
Canine patients weighing over 10kg
Patients with naive (newly diagnosed) and relapsed (pre-treated) Large Cell B-Cell lymphoma.
Must be feeling clinically WELL at home.
Must meet bloodwork requirements and have no evidence of primary gastrointestinal or lung involvement; eligibility is at the discretion of the investigator.
Patients CANNOT be receiving immunomodulatory drugs (Apoquel, mycophenolate, cyclosporine, azathioprine).
Patients must be off prednisone for a minimum of 72 hours prior to CAR-T therapy.
Benefit:
Complete cost of all treatments and rechecks are covered by study, including initial staging; up to $4,000 allotted for possible adverse events; $2,000 stipend for additional/future treatment at the VHC upon completion
You pet will contribute to development of an important cancer therapy.
To Participate:
Pet owners must be willing to transport their dog to and from the treatment center in Columbia, Missouri, for every visit abiding by specific timelines.
A full screening will be performed prior to full study enrollment.
Participation will require pets to come to our clinic for a minimum of seven visits over the first 21 days of the study, with future longer-term follow up appointments required, and/or until progression or relapse.
For more information on this study please contact: cvmclinicaltrials@missouri.edu with the subject pertaining to the trial of interest.
Thyroid Sodium Iodide Symporter
The University of Missouri Veterinary Medical Center is enrolling patients into a clinical trial to assess whether using special stains for the sodium iodide symporter can allow us to identify tumors that are taking up iodine after a thyroid tumor has been removed. This would limit the need for expensive thyroid scans before surgery and increase the number of dogs that could be considered for additional treatment if their thyroid cancer is aggressive.
Criteria:
Dogs with presumed thyroid carcinoma considered likely candidates for thyroidectomy
Patients who have received neoadjuvant radiation (external beam or I-131) or chemotherapy, exogenous iodine supplementation are not eligible.
Benefit:
The pre-operative thyroid scan would allow radioactive iodine therapy to be considered as an option following surgery, if there were concerns that your dog’s thyroid tumor was more aggressive than usual.
After enrollment, the study will contribute $1,500 to cover associated clinical costs. This includes coverage of costs associated with the pre-operative thyroid scan, including sedation and hospital care (approximately ($1,055).
To Participate:
Pet owners must be willing to move forward with surgical planning and resection of thyroid and surrounding lymph nodes.
A full screening will be performed prior to enrollment at the owner’s expense.
Responsible for initial assessment and consultation to determine eligibility for the trial.
For more information on this study please contact: cvmclinicaltrials@missouri.edu with the subject pertaining to the trial of interest.

{ "content": { "id": 29996, "headline": "Treatment of Canine Sarcoma with FAP CAR T-cells (FAP CAR-T Study)", "tagline": "New treatment with autologous FAP CAR T-cells for sarcomas", "description": "

CAR T cell therapy has fundamentally changed how certain cancers are treated. By reprogramming a patient's own T lymphocytes to express a receptor targeting a protein on tumor cells, it directs the immune system to destroy them, producing durable remissions in blood cancers once refractory to conventional treatment.


These benefits have yet to reach veterinary patients, and some cancers remain especially hard to treat with immunotherapy. Sarcomas can be very resistant to standard treatment across many species, including dogs. Led by investigators at Colorado State University, we are testing CAR T cells engineered against FAP, a protein highly expressed in many sarcomas, in pet dogs. We are evaluating both the therapy's activity and its side effects. Advancing this work meets a real clinical need for companion animals while accelerating progress for human patients as well.


In this study, we will test a new treatment for dogs with sarcomas. As the tumor has to be biopsied, this study is best for sarcomas that are external or on the outside of the body.


", "requirements": "

This new treatment uses special cells called CAR T cells, prepared as follows:

  1. We take immune cells (T cells) that fight disease in your dog's body with a blood draw
  2. We change these cells in a lab so they can find and attack cells that support the tumor's growth
  3. We give your dog oral chemotherapy (Cytoxan) over two days to reduce their natural population of immune cells
  4. We give these improved cells back to your dog through an infusion directly into the blood stream.

Developing a non-invasive treatment for canine thyroid tumors
Developing histotripsy as a non-invasive treatment for canine thyroid tumors
Principal Investigator
Bio Item
Joanne Tuohy, DVM, PhD, DACVS–Small Animal
, bio
Contacts
Robyn Fox, LVT
Clinical Trials Coordinator
Purpose
To evaluate histotripsy, a new, non-invasive way of treating canine thyroid tumors that can precisely target and destroy abnormal tissues without surgery or radiation.
Background
Up to 90% of thyroid tumors in dogs are cancerous, and the main treatment right now is surgery. The thyroid sits next to critical blood vessels and breathing tubes, creating potential complications for surgery. Furthermore, many tumors cannot be operated on at all because they are stuck to these vital structures. Histotripsy is an innovative method using focused sound waves—not heat, surgery, or radiation—to safely destroy tumor cells with millimeter accuracy. Prior studies using this technology for canine bone cancer were safe and successful. Histotripsy has the potential to be the first truly tissue-selective ablation method capable of sparing nerves, vessels, and other critical structures for thyroid tumor ablation
Eligibility
Dogs diagnosed with a thyroid tumor whose families have elected for surgical removalDogs stable enough for general anesthesia
Exclusion
Presence of other life-threatening diseasesNon-resectable thyroid tumors
Study Design
Patients that are being seen as surgical candidates for thyroid tumors will undergo standard of care workup including bloodwork and CT scan. Once deemed eligible, patients will undergo an MRI to plan for Histotripsy treatment. A single histotripsy treatment day will occur on a separate day followed by surgical resection of the tumor one day after that.
Compensation
Eligible patients that have received a surgical workup will receive the pre-planning MRI and single histotripsy treatment at no cost to the owner. In addition a $3,000 credit will be applied toward the cost of thyroid tumor resection surgery performed at our facility.
**There is a possibility for financial assistance beyond the $2,000 through a Compassionate Care Fund for cancer patients available at the Animal Cancer Care and Research Center. Care Credit is also accepted at both the Blacksburg and Roanoke facility.
